composition: The IF steel is an interstitial-free, single-phase α-ferrite (body-centred cubic iron) material, i.e. essentially free of interstitial carbon and nitrogen. Its exact chemical composition is reported only in Supplementary Table S1 of the paper and is not given in the main text. In the FEM treatment its matrix is represented as α-ferrite (α-Fe) with E = 210 GPa, ν = 0.3, lattice friction stress σ0 = 150 MPa, Taylor factor M = 3.16, shear modulus μ = 80.7 GPa, Burgers vector b = 0.248 nm, dislocation interaction constant α = 0.2, Hall–Petch slope kHP = 130 MPa μm^-1/2 and initial dislocation density 7×10^13 m^-2.
summary: The interstitial-free (IF) steel is the reference/benchmark material in a study that designs a new carbon-free, TiB2-reinforced low-density triplex steel. It is a conventional, single-phase α-ferrite steel evaluated in its as-received condition, and it serves two roles: (i) as the black reference engineering stress-strain curve in tensile comparison (Fig. 3(a)), and (ii) as the modelling benchmark for a TiB2-free α-ferrite matrix in the finite-element simulation (Figs. 2, 11). Its low strength but very high ductility frame the trade-off driving the new alloy design: strength added solely by ceramic reinforcement costs a drastic loss of ductility.
